Medical Coder Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A medical coder resume has to prove one thing above all: that your codes are right. Hiring managers at hospitals, clinics, and coding vendors do not hire on enthusiasm for healthcare. They hire on accuracy, volume, and the specialties you can code without supervision — and they check all three before they ever call you.

This guide gives you a full annotated example for a hospital inpatient coder, the credentials hiring sides actually check, and the mistakes that quietly cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works for coders: what you coded, at what volume, and with what measurable accuracy.

Quick answer: A medical coder resume should lead with your coding accuracy rate, your volume, and your CPC or CCS credential; name AAPC or AHIMA certifications; and pair each experience bullet with a count, such as charts coded per week, clean-claim rate, or denials cut.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with accuracy and volume — 99.5%, 180+ charts a week, and the CPC credential up front.
  • Prove revenue impact with clean-claim rates, denial reductions, and audit findings.
  • Name the code sets and specialties you code: ICD-10-CM/PCS, CPT, HCPCS, and your settings.
  • Every bullet pairs a duty with a count: charts per week, accuracy rate, or denials cut.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Medical Coding Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a coding manager or a HIM director and you will not hear "passionate about healthcare." You will hear:

  • Accuracy first. Your coding accuracy rate is the single number that matters most. "99.5% coding accuracy across quarterly audits" is a hiring signal; "responsible for accurate coding" is not.
  • Productivity at volume. Charts coded per day or per hour, by setting. Inpatient, outpatient, and emergency-department coding all have different expected volumes — name yours.
  • Specialty coverage. Cardiology, orthopedics, oncology, surgery, evaluation and management — the specialties you can code independently decide which desks you can sit at.
  • Denial and revenue impact. Clean-claim rates, denial reductions, and the dollars your corrections recovered. Coders who can show they protected revenue get hired first.
  • Compliance without shortcuts. HIPAA, payer rules, and audit readiness. Hiring managers want coders whose charts survive external audits, not ones who "helped with compliance."

If your resume reads like a course description — all training, no accuracy, no volume — it will lose to one that reads like an audit report.

Medical Coder Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a hospital inpatient coder with outpatient experience. It is fictional — the name and figures are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern real hiring managers respond to: what you coded, the volume, and the accuracy.

MARIAM BELLO, CPC
Atlanta, GA · (404) 555-0183 · mariam.bello@email.com

SUMMARY
Certified Professional Coder with 5 years coding inpatient and outpatient records for a 380-bed hospital, including 3 years on the inpatient team. Code 180+ inpatient charts per week at 99.5% accuracy across quarterly audits, covering cardiology, orthopedics, and general surgery; cut the team's denial rate from 9% to 4% by building a physician-query template for missing documentation. Certified Professional Coder (AAPC); ICD-10-CM/PCS and CPT proficient.

CREDENTIALS
Certified Professional Coder (CPC) — AAPC, 2021 · ICD-10-CM/PCS proficiency · HIPAA Privacy & Security training, current · AHIMA member

SKILLS
ICD-10-CM · ICD-10-PCS · CPT · HCPCS Level II · DRG assignment · MS-DRG & APR-DRG · HCC coding · Encoder systems (3M) · Electronic health records (Epic) · Physician queries · Denial management · Audit support · Medical terminology · Anatomy & physiology

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Inpatient Medical Coder — Northside General Hospital, Atlanta, GA | 2022–Present - Code 180+ inpatient charts per week across cardiology, orthopedics, and general surgery at 99.5% accuracy on quarterly internal audits - Assign MS-DRGs and sequence principal and secondary diagnoses for complex stays, including multi-day surgical admissions and comorbid cases - Cut the coding team's denial rate from 9% to 4% in one year by building a physician-query template that resolved missing documentation before claims went out - Support external payer audits by pulling and organizing coded records; the last two audits returned zero findings on charts I coded - Train 3 new coders on inpatient workflow, encoder use, and query etiquette, bringing each to full productivity within 6 weeks

Outpatient Medical Coder — Peachtree Family Clinic, Atlanta, GA | 2020–2022 - Coded 90+ outpatient encounters per day, including office visits, minor procedures, and preventive services, at 99.2% accuracy - Applied CPT and HCPCS Level II codes for evaluation and management visits, labs, and imaging, keeping the clinic's clean-claim rate above 96% - Flagged recurring documentation gaps in provider notes and fed them back to the clinic manager, cutting rework on corrected claims by a third - Managed the clinic's coding queue during a two-month EHR migration with no backlog at go-live

EDUCATION
Certificate, Medical Coding — Atlanta Technical College, 2020 B.S., Health Information Management (coursework) — Georgia State University, 2019

Why it works: the summary leads with the two numbers coding managers check first — 99.5% accuracy and 180+ charts a week — then adds the credential. Every bullet pairs a task with a result: denials down, audits clean, new coders productive. Nothing is a duty without a number.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: accuracy, volume, credential

"99.5% accuracy," "180+ charts per week," "CPC" — three facts that let a coding manager place you in thirty seconds. Lead with accuracy and volume, not with your training. If your accuracy rate is lower than you would like, lead with volume and specialty coverage instead.

Experience: accuracy proof, not duties

Each bullet should answer "what changed because you coded it?" "Coded inpatient charts" is a duty; "cut the denial rate from 9% to 4% by building a physician-query template" is proof. Accuracy rate, charts per day, clean-claim rate, denial rate, and audit findings are the five metrics coders are judged on — put at least three of them on your resume.

Credentials: put CPC where buyers look

CPC belongs in the header or summary, not buried at the bottom — it is the first filter for most coding roles. CCS (Certified Coding Specialist) is the hospital-side credential and carries weight for inpatient desks; RHIT signals health-information breadth. If you are exam-eligible but not yet certified, say so honestly ("CPC exam scheduled") rather than implying the credential.

Compliance: name the audit, not the effort

"Ensured HIPAA compliance" tells a hiring manager nothing. "Last two external payer audits returned zero findings on charts I coded" tells them everything. The same applies to query practices: name the process you followed, not the fact that you followed one.

Medical Coder Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "ICD-10-PCS" vs "ICD-10" matters to hospital filters:

  • Coding systems: ICD-10-CM, ICD-10-PCS, CPT, HCPCS Level II, DRG assignment, MS-DRG, APR-DRG, HCC coding, risk adjustment
  • Specialties: inpatient coding, outpatient coding, cardiology, orthopedics, general surgery, evaluation and management, emergency department, oncology
  • Quality & revenue: coding accuracy, clean-claim rate, denial management, physician queries, clinical documentation improvement, audit support, charge capture
  • Systems & process: 3M encoder, Epic, Cerner, EHR, abstracting, coding queue management, remote coding, productivity standards

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Hospitals and coding vendors screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. Start from a clean template like the ones at Cvyon's template gallery, or the role page for medical coders.

5 Mistakes That Cost Medical Coders Interviews

  1. Duties without accuracy numbers. "Responsible for coding patient records" could describe any coder. Add your accuracy rate, your volume, or a result (denials cut, audits passed) to every bullet.
  2. Hiding the credential. CPC or CCS is the first thing a coding manager looks for. If it sits at the bottom of page two, your resume may never reach a human. Put it in the header or summary.
  3. Listing code sets without context. "ICD-10, CPT, HCPCS" on its own says nothing. Say where you used them — inpatient cardiology, outpatient E/M, surgical cases — and at what volume.
  4. Claiming auditor scope you do not hold. Coding and auditing are different jobs. Claiming audit experience you never held fails the first reference check and can end a candidacy outright.
  5. Vague compliance language. "Ensured coding compliance" is unverifiable. Name the audit, the accuracy rate, or the outcome — or leave the line out entirely.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a CPC to become a medical coder?

Practically, yes for most roles. The CPC (from AAPC) is the credential most employers list first, and most postings require it or an equivalent such as the CCS (from AHIMA). Entry-level coders sometimes start with a certificate and CPC-A apprentice status, then drop the apprentice designation after a year of verified experience.

How do I show accuracy if my employer never gave me a rate?

Use the closest honest proxy: audit results ("zero findings on my charts in two payer audits"), clean-claim rates, denial rates, or the volume you sustained without rework. Never invent a percentage — a hiring manager can verify it, and a fabricated number ends the candidacy.

What is the difference between a medical coder and a medical biller?

Coders translate the clinical record into codes; billers submit those codes as claims and chase payment. The roles overlap in small practices but are separate jobs in hospitals. If you do both, say so and split the bullets — do not let billing duties hide your coding accuracy.

Can medical coders work remotely?

Yes — remote coding is one of the most common remote roles in healthcare. Remote postings still check the same things: accuracy, volume, specialty coverage, and a track record of working without on-site supervision.

How long should a medical coder resume be?

One page for most coders, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across genuinely different settings — inpatient, outpatient, and auditing — that each need space, and even then keep your accuracy and credential on page one.

Do I need a degree to become a medical coder?

No. Most employers ask for a coding certificate and a credential — CPC from AAPC or CCS from AHIMA — rather than a degree. Certificate programs teach ICD-10, CPT, and HCPCS, and the exam proves you can code at the standard employers audit against.
